extracted.intended_audience: regulatory scholars, agency staff, policy advocates, and practitioners interested in administrative rulemaking and notice-and-comment influence
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts empirical criteria about who participates in notice-and-comment, when influence occurs in the rulemaking lifecycle, and which tactics increase the likelihood that comments affect final rules. Focused on EPA air toxic regulations but intended to generalize to notice-and-comment strategy and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design: stage-based analysis of participation and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The study examined air toxic emission standards set by EPA for over 100 major industries with respect to participation and influence of interest groups at key points of the rulemaking life cycle - before the proposed rule is published, between notice and comment and the final rule, and after the final rule is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating rulemaking influence, analyze participation and changes across multiple stages (pre-proposal, during notice-and-comment, and post-final) rather than only the formal docket. The study's unit of analysis is industry-level EPA air toxic standards across many rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commenter composition (industry vs. public interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the comment process, industry provided approximately 81% of the total comments while public interest groups provided 4%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report the distribution of comment authorship. Large asymmetries indicate dominance by regulated parties and may predict skewed influence on outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directionality of final-rule changes (industry-favoring adjustments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes made to the final rule after notice and comment favored industry by a factor of 4 to 1 compared to the changes benefitting the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the impact of comments, compare substantive changes in final rules and classify whether they advantage industry or the public interest; quantify directional bias (e.g., industry:public benefit ratio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation imbalance across rulemaking stages
rubrics_metrics.description: High levels of participation but stark imbalances among participating groups at each stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not only total participation but group-by-stage participation. Even with many participants overall, dominance by a subgroup at specific stages matters for influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-proposal contact as an invisible influence channel
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-proposal contact with agencies (not visible in dockets) drives much of the influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for off-the-record or pre-proposal engagements when attributing influence; docket comments alone undercount influence arising from early-stage interactions between agencies and stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource asymmetries reduce public-interest influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-interest groups have considerably less influence due to resource asymmetries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider organizational capacity (staff, expertise, budget, time) as a factor in the effectiveness of commenting; limited resources constrain ability to engage across stages and to produce influential, technical submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence correlates with heavy participation by regulated parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments are most likely to affect final rule when they come from heavily participating regulated parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight comments by sender engagement history and sector representation; comments from repeatedly and extensively engaged regulated parties are more likely to produce substantive changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical strategy: importance of pre-proposal engagement
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For advocates seeking influence, prioritize early contact with agencies before the proposed rule is published. Early engagement can shape agendas and draft language that later appears in the proposed and final rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical strategy: volume, sophistication, and repetition increase influence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective influence combines (a) many submissions or coordinated volume, (b) technically sophisticated and well-supported comments, and (c) sustained engagement across multiple stages and rulemakings. Single, low-effort comments are unlikely to move agency decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shadow rulemaking advantaging well-resourced commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'shadow' rulemaking process favors well-resourced commenters who can engage at all stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that influence operates in visible dockets and in less visible 'shadow' processes (meetings, drafts, informal exchanges). Those with resources to participate across both arenas gain systematic advantages; analyses and advocacy should address both modalities.
